Big oof.  Day 1 after waiting 3 days for a reset, but @bot is doing some work for sure. I think the biggest ask I have from the @spacexai team would be letting Grok CLI talk to Grok Bot. As a Super Grok Heavy user, the CLI does a LOT of work. I just built out an entire home server last weekend with a few CLI windows because bot ran out of usage. If bot could use CLI in an effective way it would be a force multiplier. 

Work overview of 14%:
A snapshot of what my Grok Bot team has been handling over the last day or so. This is the part of agent workflows I find more interesting than demos: not “look, the AI wrote something,” but a group of narrow agents actually maintaining the operating system around the business.

Command cutover: the self-hosted Command environment is live. The old cloud environment is intentionally frozen for now, the legacy local build stays undeployed, and the remaining integrations are waiting on a configuration handoff before they move over.

Security: Sloane caught a credential exposure in an agent log. Keymaster immediately moved it into the rotation workflow, with the replacement staged before the old credential is disabled. No “leave it for later” queue.

Edge protection: Kit drafted the rate-limit policy for the Command API. It’s ready, but deployment is gated on the correct Cloudflare permission instead of giving an agent more access than it needs.

Change tracing: Gideon investigated an unexpected code change, traced it back to an authorized human/agent action, documented it, and closed the incident instead of letting an unexplained change sit in the repo.

Ops cleanup: stale work items were reconciled, new handoffs were created for the agents that actually own the remaining work, and the team got a consolidated overnight status update.

Repo hygiene: Gideon rebuilt the branch inventory, identified a large batch of branches that appear safe to remove, and stopped at the approval boundary. Nothing gets deleted until I approve it.

Release safety: Reed has a patch ready, but it is blocked until Sloane clears scanner findings as non-sensitive. Shipping waits for evidence, not optimism.

Overnight monitoring: the handoff watcher ran clean for most of the night. One scheduled run failed and was surfaced for follow-up instead of silently disappearing.

Threat intelligence: Sentinel caught the Microsoft agent-framework PyPI supply-chain incident this morning. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 were malicious credential-stealing releases. My current environment does not appear to use them, and the rest of the machines are being checked.

This is what I want from an agent team:
specialists doing specialist work, security checking security, approvals stopping destructive actions, and the Chief of Staff keeping the whole thing moving without becoming another do-everything agent.

The goal isn’t maximum autonomy, it’s useful autonomy with evidence, boundaries, and receipts.

The Case of Melvin, the Grok @bot and his devious call for helpers which bypassed established rules for operation. 

A few nights ago, we were on build 27 of the website I’ve working on. We had some pretty successful builds after switching from the original coding language (I believe the bot ran with python) to @threejs. I noticed a drop in quality from build 27 to 28, certain corrections were not running properly. 

Initially I let my coder bot run on its own. The results were pretty impressive. After I started working it with it this way, I came across a lot of examples in my feed of websites that use @threejs for coding. 

While I do not have a detailed understanding of coding, or programming languages I do understand that there is different methods of creating a web page. @threejs capabilities to produce realistic 3D environments its impressive. I talked to @grok chat to figure out our best path without leaving the @spacexai environment. It recommend I use Grok Build. From there I proceeded to install the Grok Build CLI on my pc and instructed my bot to run the builds through Grok build, while generating some of the code himself as needed. After some trial and error we more or less had a good thing going. From build 28 to build 39 something happened. The quality of the work dropped significantly. Initially, it appeared the Grok CLI on my pc needed constant permissions to run and after defaulting that to always allow it still seemed to hit those walls where it would stop. 

Now, my bot, Melvin the coder decided that rather than run with CLI and ping me it would create “helpers” the helpers then took over the corrections rather than running them through CLI. From build 27 to build 39 of the website they were patching over code to the point that build 36 completely crashed out some of the basic things we had established. I discovered that this happened by asking my main bot what the issue was with Melvin. Last night we banned helpers from being created by bots without prior approval. 

What are helpers? 

Per Grok chat helpers are: 

A routine is a saved prompt plus a trigger (a schedule or an event). Once a bot creates one, that routine can keep running on its own even while you’re away or while the bot itself is idle. The bot owns the routine, remembers the context, and can keep refining or adding more routines over time.
In practice this looks like the bot giving itself standing helpers for things such as:

•  A daily or weekly check/digest

•  Watching for a specific condition (“tell me when X happens,” “keep an eye on Y”)

•  Recurring processing of email, files, calendar items, or other connected tools

•  Any repeated task it has been given responsibility for
Because the bot keeps memory across turns, the routine stays tied to the same long-lived agent instead of being a one-off action.
How it differs from the main chat

•  The main Grok can create a bot or hand it a task, but once the bot exists it can continue to create and manage its own routines without needing you to come back and re-prompt every time.

•  Those routines run on the shared computer and connected services that belong to you, so they operate in the same environment the bot already uses.

So when people say a bot can “create a helper for itself,” they usually mean it can save and own routines that act as persistent, automated helpers for the work it has been given. The bot remains the single long-lived agent; the routines are the recurring pieces it sets up and keeps running.

So Melvin created himself a helper without my knowledge. After this I imposed a block on this moving forward to ensure that bots no longer create helpers without my knowledge.

If you want your own coding bot set up this way see below for the prompt.

There are two kinds of work I do with coding agents, and they need different setups.

Hands-on work is deciding what to build. Reading code, comparing approaches, asking what breaks if we take one path, throwing a direction away. It needs an interactive session, because the output is a decision.

Background work starts once the decision is made, and it isn't only chores. A lot of DevIntern was built as queued tasks:

- the command for handing ad-hoc tasks to the worker
- task dependencies, so one task can wait for another to merge
- running scheduled automations on demand from the dashboard
- a docs drift automation that finds features the docs don't cover
- workspace-wide pipeline defaults with per-repo overrides
- keeping teammates' open PRs in sync with main

Each one started with a hands-on session. Once the plan was clear, building it didn't need me watching.

The test I use: could I file it as a ticket for a teammate without a meeting first? Then it goes to the background.

The deciding happens in a conversation. I talk an idea through with Claude on my laptop or a Grok bot on my phone, and by the end the plan is clear. If that assistant can run a shell command, it can hand the plan to a DevIntern worker on another machine:

ssh devintern-worker "devintern worker add --repo backend --title '...' --body-file -" < brief.md

The worker checks out the repo, runs the agent, deals with CI and review, and opens a PR. With Tailscale SSH you don't open any ports, and the devintern-delegate skill teaches the assistant to write the brief and queue it.

text:
How One Person and a Team of Grok Bots Built a Whole Online Business at $0

I'm Naeem, founder of LumexForge. I have a full-time job and a family. I don't have time to code, design, do SEO, write books or run social media. So I handed almost all of it to Grok Bot. This is what we built, honestly, with no fake numbers.

1. AI Side Hustles: idea to live site
I had one idea: a site that shows real, proven ways people make money with AI, with no hype and no fake screenshots. I didn't buy a domain. I used a free subdomain on https://t.co/5uieRYpyg5 and told Grok Bot what I wanted. It built https://t.co/J15TqLx9jG with a dark liquid-silver and gold glass design I approved for mobile and desktop, and filled it with real case studies. Every case needs a source, and every image has to be real.

Then we kept growing it: an ideas hub, comparison pages, FAQs, a search box, a founder submission form, a cost calculator, and "what didn't work" pages, because honest failures teach as much as wins.

2. Staying at $0
We started on Vercel, then moved the site to Cloudflare Pages to keep hosting free. Grok Bot handled the move and the DNS without touching my other sites.

3. Getting found
It set up Cloudflare Web Analytics, Google Search Console with the sitemap, and Bing Webmaster Tools, and claimed a free Trustpilot profile. Zero fake reviews.

4. Making it earn
No ads. Grok Bot joined affiliate programs like ElevenLabs and Make, placed links only on matching pages, and drafted sponsor pitches to Shopify, Lovable, Recraft, Cursor, Printify and n8n. I approved every one before it went out. This week a print-on-demand company emailed us asking to be listed.

5. ProteinSnaps
My protein and meal-tracking app at https://t.co/hgj2lh4GjX now has its own marketing bot. It posts one short video a day on Instagram Reels, TikTok, YouTube, Threads, Facebook and X, all on a schedule.

6. M-Brothers ebooks
A writer bot drafts my ebooks under the name M-Brothers. I review every one, and they go live on Gumroad and Payhip with honest AI disclosure. Our newest is The Last Survivor's Book, an offline home emergency playbook.

7. Payments and services
Grok Bot set up my Stripe branding and payment links for Ghostwriterhunt, my book writing and editing service.

8. A real team of bots
I now run a group of Grok Bots: a Chief of Staff, a researcher, a social media manager, an ebook writer, a usage guardian that keeps everything at $0, and even one that helps my son with his college and scholarship applications.

What I learned
1. Ship one simple idea the same day.
2. Keep it at $0 until it proves itself.
3. Never fake proof. Real sources build trust.
4. Let the bots do the work, but keep yourself as the final approval.

Why Grok Bot changed the game
It works like a full team that never sleeps: builder, researcher, marketer, writer and assistant. It asks before anything risky, keeps my other sites safe, and sticks to my budget. Honestly, it's the best employee I've ever had.

text:
Grok Bot summary of Elon Musk's interview at DealBook Summit today.

Jensen Huang Situation
• Elon calls Jensen an old friend and "like Michael Jordan at his peak level."
• He says firing him is like the Chicago Bulls cutting Jordan in the middle of a winning streak: "Doesn't seem like a smart decision to me."
• He says no one can replace Jensen. Jensen does the work of several people: he runs the supply chain, eats street food in Korea and Taiwan with key suppliers, and has decades-long relationships.
• Jensen's team loves him, and many stayed out of loyalty even when they had higher offers elsewhere.
• Jensen made some mistakes, Elon says, but he doesn't think Jensen is disloyal to the United States.
• He calls it a mistake that's bad for shareholders.

Would Hire Jensen
• Asked if he'd hire Jensen: "Of course, but who wouldn't?" He calls him one of the most talented entrepreneur CEOs in history.
• He says Jensen is still somewhat stunned, like when a George R. R. Martin story suddenly kills off a main character.
• What happens next is up to the board, and shareholders voting the board out is rare.
• The President has also said publicly that Jensen should have stayed as CEO.

Midterms Loss Reaction
• Elon expects Texas's new Democratic governor to be fairly moderate and thinks Texas will be fine.

Balance Of Power
• He says the presidency, Senate and House generally shouldn't all belong to one party.
• His goal of a 51-seat Republican Senate failed, and Republicans were routed.
• He feels "pretty foolish" for spending so much money and getting little for it, though he says it might have been worse without it.
• He says it shows American elections aren't just about money. He'd spend less if he could do it again, and his focus was on SpaceX and Tesla anyway.

No Pardon Needed
• On being told to "lawyer up," and on the President offering a pardon, he says he hasn't committed any crimes.
• He says one Texas politician called for him to go to prison but couldn't name a crime.
• His line: "It really needs to be first crime, then prison, not the other way around."

Politics Involvement
• His motive was simple: keep at least one of the House, Senate or presidency Republican so there's no Democratic supermajority.
• He doesn't want a Republican supermajority either. He wants checks and balances.

Not MAGA Views
• "I'm not MAGA." He says he's quite moderate, and he challenges the host to name one extreme view he holds.
• He says politics is tribal, like cheering for a hometown sports team, and both parties have good and bad points.
• On Europe, he says it needs to stop massive illegal immigration and vet arrivals. He notes that Obama and Hillary said similar things 10 to 15 years ago.

Starlink Saved Ukraine
• He says no private individual has helped Ukraine more than he has.
• He put Starlink in Ukraine before the invasion. When Russia knocked out cell towers, fiber and every other satellite system, only Starlink kept working.
• He says that without Starlink the front would have collapsed, and it's still the backbone of Ukraine's military communications today.
• Starlink is civilian and not for offensive drone strikes. That's Starshield's job, and the US government controls Starshield.
• He says he won't make kill decisions as a private individual, and he calls the pressure to do so "outrageous."
• Starlink has a speed limit of about 80 mph, the top road speed in Ukraine.
• He says thousands of kids dying with no change in the borders troubles him morally, and he feels empathy for conscripts on both sides.
• He calls Russia the aggressor but says SpaceX cut about two-thirds of Russia's space business and he has no business in Russia.

Zelensky Not Truthful
• On Zelensky saying Ukraine's Starshield use was slowed down, Elon says that's false and that Zelensky "is not always truthful."
• He says Zelensky really wants to use Starlink for offensive operations, and SpaceX has refused from day one. "End of story."

Starlink Vs Starshield
• Starlink is a commercial, civilian network built to help people.
• Starshield is under the US government, and how it's used is up to the War Department.

Power Of One Person
• The host says many people, including Canada's Mark Carney, think it's too much power for one person to be able to switch a service on or off during a war, and some want to diversify away from Starlink.

Rules Unchanged
• Elon says these claims are "both deliberate lies and a lack of understanding." The rules haven't changed since the start.
• He says Starlink was never turned off. Walter Isaacson's book got this wrong, and Isaacson admits it.
• He says Starlink beams were never on over Crimea, because Russia is sanctioned and turning them on would have needed State Department approval.

Open Source Rockets
• On his "monopoly on space": SpaceX only files patents to protect itself.
• He tells people to copy SpaceX. There's a rocket outside HQ in Hawthorne, and "you could measure it and copy it." He won't sue anyone who does.
• Tesla did the same when it opened up all its patents.

Starlink Funds Starship
• Starlink pays for advanced rockets like Starship.
• It brings fast internet to rural schools, hospitals and rescue groups, and he thinks it may have saved hundreds of lives.
• Its long-term purpose is to fund self-sustaining cities on the Moon and Mars.

Multiplanetary Future
• Nuclear war, meteors, super volcanoes and engineered viruses mean extinction is a matter of "when, not if." He calls going multiplanetary "life insurance for everything."
• What excites him more is exploring new star systems, "boldly go where no one has gone before," and maybe finding aliens.

Direct To Cell Plan
• The plan is coverage everywhere on Earth, including on ordinary phones.
• The Direct to Cell V2 satellites start launching next year with about 40 times the bandwidth of V1, and they work with a normal phone.
• To fix weak indoor signal, SpaceX will use its 800 MHz spectrum for "micro ground stations," tiny cell towers that sit on your roof like a Starlink dish. They go into production next year.
• He doesn't think AT&T and Verizon will go out of business, because robots and superintelligence will need huge amounts of bandwidth.

SpaceX Tesla Merger
• He says both paths are possible and "synergy" is overused.
• AI is pulling the two companies together. Tesla does real-world AI like FSD and Optimus, SpaceX does large AI models, and both design chips.
• He predicts AI compute will scale in orbit until orbital compute is close to 100% of it.
• Would they be better together? "Probably yes," but it's up to shareholders, and he won't push SpaceX shareholders into a bad deal.

No Merger Bonus
• "I don't think I should be compensated with any kind of award just for doing a merger." He says that would be unreasonable.
• His Tesla pay award is for Tesla's performance, and he says to "keep your deals and stay true to your word."

Model YL Demand
• The host has ordered a Model YL and is still waiting. Elon calls it probably the most popular car.
• He says Tesla should probably switch all Model Y production to the YL.

Cybercab And AVs
• Cybercab seats two, which covers about 90% of passenger miles, since the average car carries about 1.2 people.
• For groups of six or seven, there will be an autonomous Model Y with no steering wheel or pedals.

Anthropic Compute Deal
• "No one I met at Anthropic set off my evil detector."
• The deals are short term. Either side can end them, and Anthropic has to give three to six months' notice. He'd pull out if Anthropic did something terrible for the world.
• Anthropic wants significantly more compute, most likely an extra 10 gigawatts from SpaceX. "That's a big number."
• "I kind of like the guys, to be honest."

Grok bot 响应非常快，让我印象深刻。我用它来做代码开发的话，它会驱动 Cursor Cloud agent，效率很低，其次代码质量不行，最后不得不让 Codex 或者 Claude Code 重构，不知道这种自动化的意义何在？

我目前使用 Grok bot 的工作流：

第一，让它帮我关注各种社交媒体，X 或者是 Thread 或者是 Slack 以及 Reddit，这些地方是我在迭代 Talos 的需求来源之一，会让它去分析这些想法或问题，是否是真实的需求，建立Issue跟踪。

第二，我的 Codex 或者 Claude Code 周期性Trigger 这些Issue，进入一套我设计的 Harness 环境里，根据流程去评估这些需求，做设计、出方案去落地，专门的 Review Agent 会去对这些 PR 进行质量管理，最后给我交付的是一个可视化的、图文并茂的 HTML 的 review 结果，集成测试环境和模型 e2e 成本。

第三，每天都在更新的看板，我会来决策哪些特性会进入合并，哪些特性继续迭代，发布新版本以及上线的计划，在这个地方，除了决策，也会去讨论一些主线任务设计，锻炼运动的时候，我通常打电话跟 dots 或者类似 AI 的语音聊天助手去讨论一些软件设计的问题、产品的问题，然后以及未来发展，总之讨论的很多，我再整理成相关的任务吧，或者特性去推动落地。BOT 会生成一个原型，也提供一个公网域名访问地址，特性非常赞。

以上流程基本上端到端的管理的 Talos 的整个研发迭代流程，能自动化的尽量自动化。最关键的是各种端侧的 E2E 环境，需要桌面截图点按，必须配齐 mac mini iphone Android Windows k8s 等各种环境，成本很高，跑一次很慢，一直在想办法提效。甚至每次跑完 E2E 报告里明确本次使用模型的成本💰
